utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not able to hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with that paper.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are still not able to hear the witness. We can hear the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Witness, we have some technical problems. Would you please make your solemn declaration again for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the witness could please be shown a piece of paper. And if he could confirm that this is his name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is my first name and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, obviously don't mention your name in the course of this testimony, and I will not do so as well and nobody in the courtroom. So I will just call you witness or sir. Just two preliminary questions in open session. What's your nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in which country are you currently living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I'm living in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could move into private session just for three questions to his background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe in one or two sentences to the Judges your educational background.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I completed the electro-technical high school in Tuzla. Weak electric current it's called. And in 1989 I completed the faculty at the University of Sarajevo after which I earned the title of teacher of technical education.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where are you currently employed, with which organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm working in the intelligence and security service of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did this organisation have a different name in previous years, and if so, what was the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. For the past several years, I don't know, but certainly from 1980 it was called the national security -- the state security service. And then in 1986, I think, it was called the Agency for Research and Documentation. After that, last year it was transformed into an organisation which is called the Intelligence Security Service of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you are and have been a member of the state security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. I'm working in the service of the state security from 1982 and I am still employed in that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't mean to interfere, but he indicated that he works for the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That means one of the entities. State, as I understand it, there's only one state and that is a state of Bosnia and Herzegovina which has these two entities. So he's only working for the entity and not the state currently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe Mr. Waespi could ask a question to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, if you could please explain for which entity, one being the Federation Bosnia and the Croatian part of Bosnia, and the other Republika Srpska, for which entity are you working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. The Federation, just like Republika Srpska comprises of all the nations and ethnic groups. I'm currently working in the Federation. These two services at the moment exist both in Republika Srpska. There is a service there as well. I don't know exactly what it's called. The secret service of Republika Srpska. And there is also the so-called intelligence security service of the Federation, which at the moment comprises the Croatian and the Bosniak component. As far as I know there are activities under way now to unite the Republika Srpska security service and our service into one service which should start operations from January of next year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like you to focus on the war period, specifically from December 1994 onwards, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. In December 1994 I was the so-called chief of a section, which was called the section for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic activities. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you just stated that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You just stated that you were concerned with intercepted messages, so in your words the purpose of this unit was what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I will try to explain it briefly. We were aware that we -- that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, nor us, had any sophisticated equipment in order to perform our jobs with any level of quality. So we believed if we used a larger number of devices, almost amateur devices, we would achieve better results. And that is why we also started this work in order to gather intelligence, data, related to our service. This location was convenient, it was favourable, and that is why we went and began to work at that location. All the more so because we did not have any rear units or other units which could offer logistical support for us, and this is why we came to this facility where the army was already located, a unit of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, Witness, whom were you monitoring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Our primary objective was to try from civilian structures, because we are a civilian intelligence service, to acquire intelligence data which would relate to our sphere of work. But when we went out to this location, we were actually able to see that all of this was interconnected, so that practically we gathered all of the intelligence information which was of interest and we passed that on to our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us whom exactly, whose lines of communication you were monitoring.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. We monitored the so-called radio relay links in the possession of the Army of Republika Srpska at the time. As far as I know they were classical army communications. Since they also lacked civilian telephone communications, they relied also on a certain number of civilian telephone lines, so that these routes then enabled us to hear many people from the civilian structures. So our objective was to intercept these communications, frequencies. There was also a lower frequency. These were UKT connections, which were used in the police service, also the army -- in army communications, then there were also conversations from hand-operated telephones, wireless telephones, ultra short wave connections, which were also possible -- and it was possible to pick them up in certain environments. So I think this is a sufficient explanation of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Within the VRS, were you focusing on specific units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: We often searched the frequency spectrums which the enemy forces used for their operations. After this searching, we made a selection and then we decided which frequency would be covered thoroughly and monitored. Since there was an army unit there, we had an agreement with them not to cover the same tasks. So in these searches, I can't remember the dates, we also found a frequency which was directly connected to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Besides that frequency, we -- when we had time and room and if the frequency was inactive in the sense that there were no conversations ongoing, then we would also monitor some other frequencies and monitor some other conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sir, do you know did the VRS also have anti-electronic warfare units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. The army of Republika Srpska had such units and they also inherited all the technical equipment from the former JNA that they had used. I know that they had these devices. Unfortunately we did not have such devices and we had to convert some other devices into devices which would be compatible and from which we could monitor these conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did the VRS realise that their communications were being intercepted by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Often from their conversations we were aware that they knew that we were doing this, but from some conversations that we heard from their top leaders and after some clumsy transmissions via radio at that time, we heard comments that we were actually receiving this from some states, which were actually passing this on to us. So that would be the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you also intercept encrypted lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, you can intercept everything on those frequencies, but it's a question of what could be decoded and what could not. We intercepted everything, open lines, we would pick that up. The encrypted lines we would try to decipher. Some things were not encrypted in the classical sense. They were encrypted by transferring certain terms or substituting certain terms, so we tried to do it in that way as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Why did the participants to these communications not use coded language or communications? Why did they talk in openness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: We often heard them asking, "Is this a secure conversation, secure line?" And if somebody was not really an expert in that would say, "Yes, it's a secure line." In other cases they would say, "Well, it's not secure," and then they would say, "Well, hopefully they're not listening to us." And then they would carry on with what they were saying. Another case was that they truly, I think in the second half of 1995 -- excuse me, I don't know the exact date, I have it written down somewhere. They used so-called encrypted telephones which could actually code speech. So then they would sometimes say, well, let's go to a secure line and then they would move to that line. But it's a part of the human nature to say something to the effect of, "Well, hopefully they're not listening to us now," and then they would still go ahead and say what they wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: (redacted). In order not to repeat myself, it's good that we had the logistics, we had food, we had security. So we were able to just devote ourselves to our actual work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said you would often spend time at this location. In July 1995, were you there all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you say "town," which town do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a couple of times that the army was up on that hill as well. Did you share the same building or were you separate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: There is only one building in that location, and that is a former JNA building. And it's quite convenient or suitable for that kind of work. We got only one room in which we worked, ate, and slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, briefly turning to technical equipment and I'm going to show you a couple of pictures later, you and the army, did you basically use the same type of equipment or was it different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: It was mainly the same equipment. Actually, there was several people who made these combinations first, and then we would just multiply these combinations. I mentioned it wasn't sophisticated equipment that we were using. It was practically amateur equipment. And it's practically the same as the ones the army used, perhaps it was a little bit newer or a little bit older, but it was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said a while ago that there was some coordination between you and the army unit, a location of frequency if I understood you correctly. Can you tell us a little bit more, but still as brief as you can, about the type of coordination, exchange of information, if that happened, you had experienced.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: We saw that there was a lot of work to do up there during our surveillance or reconnaissance. We saw that there were a lot of frequencies on that so-called RRU-800. And each frequency had 24 channels. So if we were to cover that in the best possible manner, we should have had the same amount of devices. Since we didn't have the appropriate number of equipment or staff, we tried to agree amongst ourselves that we should not be doing the same tasks, and the data that we received should be exchanged, mutually, so that both sides would receive the total amount of information. So all the information that I received I passed on to the army, and all the information, hopefully, the army passed back to me. And then we would pass this information on to our centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would like now to go into the procedures you and your unit used when listening to conversations. Can you please tell the Judges what you did once you had I guess your headphones on. Can you tell us step by step the procedures you and your unit used.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: We had a room in which we had three different combinations of equipment that we used. You had two people manning the equipment, and those people would be listening. One of the devices was for the duty officer in case there was a conversation on the frequency of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska. If there was a conversation on that frequency, it would immediately be recorded. As for the other combinations, we monitored, or rather, the machine was scanning conversations. And as soon as we heard someone talk, we would stop right there and start recording the conversation. In time, we concluded that certain channels on these frequencies corresponded with certain meanings, or rather, certain people. So these channels would be watched with special attention. And if there was nothing else happening on the other frequencies of channels, we would listen to that specific channel and wait for a conversation to start. As soon as a conversation began, we would start the reel-to-reel recorder, the UHER, and we would tape record the conversation. Following the recording of the conversation, every conversation proved to be particularly crucial or containing urgent priority information, we would use a different, another UHER machine we had there, a reel-to-reel recorder which we used to reproduce the conversations. We would play the conversation back. We would transcribe it on to a computer, after which we sent this to our centre. If it was no urgent conversation, we would just mark it, adding the date, time, and frequency of the conversation, after which -- on the UHER there is a counter which measures the length of the reel of the tape. It has numbers to measure that. You have the beginning and the end which made it easier for us to play back the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said that you would record it and also put it into a computer. Did you also transcribe it on to a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. Normally if something was urgent and if the recording was a good-quality recording, if the sound was clear, we would immediately start transferring information into a computer. If we realised that it would entail a certain amount of effort to play back, we would take everything down on a piece of paper which we later used to transcribe everything into a computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What happened to these pieces of paper? Were they preserved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: We only preserved a certain number of those. Whenever we went to a different location near the building where we burned those papers, or rather, documents, we would go there and burn them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you use notebooks of any kind to record these intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, we did. I had a notebook, we called it notebook. It was a leather-bound black notebook. For a while we used this to register the frequencies that we found during our searches. It was also used to note down certain procedures in setting the radio devices. Furthermore, it was used to record all the conversations that had been played back encrypted and forwarded according to the numbers that we had determined. There was yet another notebook which I don't have with me here that was also used for monitoring electronic surveillance. It was very much like the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How about the contents of the communication? Would you also have a notebook in which you recorded the same information, I believe you said, was put into the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: No. We had no notebook to reproduce that, because reproduce is the term we used to play back the conversations. We reproduced these conversations on some pieces of paper, those that we had at the time, because we had a shortage of paper to use for writing. We didn't have enough blank paper, so we often used other kinds of paper. This would entail a lengthy explanation, however the answer is no, we didn't take that down into notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know whether the army, whom you said were located at the same place, used notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I do remember that they had some kind of notebooks, and sometimes I envied them for that. They did have notebooks. I know that I saw notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that you would write the information down on a piece of paper. Can you tell us what exactly you wrote down on that piece of paper and eventually on the computer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. The moment we caught the beginning of a conversation we would immediately write down the date and time of the beginning of the conversation. We would also record the frequency, the channel being used, as well as the participants. On the basis of these elements, we later put together some kind of heading containing all this information that we'd previously written down on a piece of paper. If you look at those, you will see that dates, such and such time, such and such these people took part in a conversation that was recorded. So this contained elements that we established at the very beginning of a conversation. Probably you would have a list of participants, or rather, at the end of the conversation you had a list of people processing the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us the time that elapses between listening to a conversation and putting it into the computer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: It very much depended. As I said before, if the information was urgent, the rule was to process them immediately, to reproduce them immediately, and forward them immediately. These conversations were bearer marks saying very urgent. As for other information that the operator on the spot did not think was urgent, could wait for other information to be collected, to be gathered, and for the army also to bring their own information, their own material, to be forwarded to our centre. So then all these would be sent in one batch, but there was no specific time at which we forwarded this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said earlier and you just repeated that that you would send these messages, I think you said, to a centre. Can you explain what centre that is and how you did that sending process.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: All the information that we obtained up there was forwarded to a centre. The centre, what I call the centre, is the seat of my company, but to make it clearer, the seat was in Tuzla and there was several ways to send the information on, to pass it on. At one time, I can't say which time precisely now, I had no communications equipment. And in that period I used the military communications system. They would forward information to the seat of their company, and then the communications operator, the signalsman there, would call my operator from the communications centre in Tuzla who would then go there to collect this information on a floppy. This is how it worked for a while throughout a certain period of time. Whenever I could, I used my own communications equipment to do this. Sometimes you would have a technical problem or a glitch, but you never had problems on both at the same time, my system and the military system, so we were always able at every single point in time to pass the information on to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how was that done in normal times? I think you said you -- at times you had to use the military communications system. How did your system work, if it worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: For some time, I was able to send my reports via an ultra short wave system through the radio modem using an ultra short wave frequency that was there, that was available. We had a direct link to Tuzla. Later on I obtained a telephone modem because I did have a telephone line, which made it possible to step up the level of secrecy. This was a more protected medium and the speed of transfer was much higher, so this was a more modern type of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And would you send that information --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Would you send that information open to Tuzla or did you treat it in one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I forgot to say this: Every single piece of information had to be encrypted first of all. Those that we sent through the military system were encoded using our own encryption programme that had been devised by our company and we were free to use it. This was an encryption programme. As soon as you had an encrypted file, this file would have a specific meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you say an "encrypted file," did you send each message, intercepted message, on its own through this encryption process or did you have a file, as I understand it, in which several messages were collected together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: There were cases of both. Sometimes you had a file containing a single report, whereas at other times you had files containing 12, 13, or more reports. It depended. If it was an urgent message, a message classified as very urgent, this would normally be passed on immediately and the file would contain only one report. Sometimes we collected reports and then sent them together encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before we go to specific exhibits, let me ask you a couple of general questions. Did your unit make efforts to be accurate in transcribing what you listened to, and if so, how do you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. The most important thing was the authenticity of information and timely information, that's what they taught us back in our company. It was very important for the message to be thoroughly authentic. It sometimes happened that there was certain sections of the conversation that we couldn't hear clearly due to background noise. There was several factors affecting this, how good the propagation was, the atmosphere. Most of the conversations were reproduced exactly as we heard them. If there was something that we weren't certain about, we would just put dots. The dots meant that this particular section of the conversation was not understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that it was very important that the message be authentic. Why was it important for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Well, I assumed because of its usefulness. It would have been very dangerous and very damaging if we wrote down something that was not accurate. And probably the army monitoring the movement of units would have been tempted to alarm certain units that were not supposed to be alarmed and we could have had people doing things they were not necessarily supposed to be doing. That's why it was crucial for every piece of information to be authentic. And if there was some kind of deficiency that was inherent in a message, this had to be made very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Talking about the participants of these conversations, were you able to identify the speakers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: There were several ways in which we were able to identify the speakers, but sometimes for different reasons we couldn't. Very often we were in a position to hear people introducing themselves at the beginning of the conversation. One of the participants would say, my name is so and so, can I please speak to so and so. So that's how we obtained information on their identities. And sometimes after a longer period of time listening to some participants, we found ourselves in a situation where we were able to identify their voices. Sometimes it was also the case that we monitored other frequencies that were also being tapped into by the military. And sometimes we called up the military because they were only doing that, and then we would ask them who is this talking on this frequency, and then they would say, well, that's, you know, who. And they would say X and Y, they would use X and Y as a code for these persons. Sometimes they would use their own recordings to identify those people, and sometimes when we were able to identify the participants, we would send information back to them calling participants X and Y. For instance, at that point in time it was less important who did what. What was more important was the operation itself, what was being done, and what was happening. That's why we didn't really put an enormous effort into tracking specific participants down. If someone was away for some time we didn't really pay attention to that. What really mattered was the content of their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We will later see examples when you identified speakers. If you couldn't identify a speaker, how would you mark the participants? You may have mentioned it before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. In that case the participants in a conversation would be given names X and Y, which meant unidentified speakers. Sometimes you had speakers whose identity was known and sometimes they were unidentified. Sometimes you would hear a voice and you would know immediately who it was and sometimes you didn't. So depending on a specific case, there were different combinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you have on one side the cases when you identified the speakers by name, on the other side you had X and Y. Now, how sure were you when you, in fact, identified the speakers and put their name on paper, on computer. Can you tell us the degree of certainty?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm going to have to object. That calls for speculation. He may be able to answer in his mind how accurate his voice identification was, but he can't answer for any other intercepts in his unit there -- intercepters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we just want to hear what the witness is going to tell us. That is his view --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Of his own personal voice identification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: -- procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Personally I worked in the way I have just described. If I was 100 per cent certain, I would put a name to the voice. What I expressly told my subordinates was not to speculate about names because it didn't matter. It was not essential for us at the time who was doing what. What really mattered was what was being done and what the result of that action would be. It was important and determined the developments that followed, but for us it didn't matter. We insisted on names being 100 per cent certain. If we couldn't put a name to a voice, well what could we do about that? We knew there were certain channels used by a specific person, but if we could not identify the person, we would just put an X. Sometimes there was a courier on a certain frequency. Sometimes it was someone's secretary. So whoever it was, if we couldn't pin him down with 100 per cent certainty, we would just put an X.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I would like you to be shown two exhibits, 319 and 320. And if it could be put on the ELMO. Do you recognise this device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. You have two devices here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what these devices were used for.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The rather large device, which we can see in this photo, at the back has a small box called "converter." This small is put together by hand. It was not professionally manufactured, so it received a signal from the antenna, and here the signal was converted into a different kind of signal which would then enter the radio device, carrying 24 different frequencies and distributing these 24 frequencies, or rather, separating these 24 different frequencies. These 24 frequencies, or channels, meant 24 different phones, telephone sets. You can't see it in this picture, but there is a cable which would bring the signal from this device and transfer it to the UHER recording device. This other piece of equipment on the right-hand side of the picture was used for different purposes, for different types of frequency, for different types of conversation. It could receive the signal directly from the antenna and we would then hear the signal using this device. We used this device to transfer the signal to a recording device and get the sound -- the signal recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. If you could have a look at the next exhibit, 320, and explain to the Court what this is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: This is the UHER reel-to-reel recorder that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that was used when you listened to a specific intercept, you would press one of these buttons. That's the procedure you followed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: When we listened or monitored, we would press the second one from left to right, and the second one from right to left. I hope that my memory is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I think the exhibits can be returned. And while this is being done, can you tell us, sir, what happened to the tapes, these reel-to-reel tapes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: In the early days at Okresanica, there were a smaller number of interesting conversations, but when we had interesting conversations, we would tape record them and then occasionally take them to our centre. We physically went there and took the tapes. As soon as there was an increasing number of interesting conversations, we would record these interesting conversations on one tape, all of them, which we would then occasionally take to the centre. The tape was packed in some sort of wrapping containing a slip of paper, which contained a date. And there was a reading from the counter locating the different conversations in the tape and their participants. I clearly remember that we sent such tapes back to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now let me turn to what you have called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to turn now to the cooperation between you and the army. And you said that you would exchange information mutually, I think was your word. Now, can you tell us briefly what happened when your unit received information from the army, intercepts which have been listened by the army; how did you process that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Whenever we received processed conversations from the army, usually on a floppy disk, we would put the floppy into your computer. We would open the document. They had their own heading, a large heading, taking up quite a lot of space on the page. We would just delete this and insert our own number and date. We would just copy the date. We would also note that this was received from the PEB unit of the 2nd Corps. I think that's what we would usually add. A sentence, all in all, which specified we had received the document from the military and that it was not ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again, once you had received this information, did you keep it for yourself or did you also send it to the centre, as you had indicated earlier about your own intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. We would encrypt it in the same way that we encrypted our own files and then pass this on to our centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have concluded the first part, more general. We'll now go into a couple of specific exhibits. So if the witness could now be shown Exhibit P347. And it should be the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you first, sir, did you spend some time with me and my investigators in my office and go over a bundle of intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, we were together and I did look at those intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the document in front of you, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I see there are some markings on it. Can you explain -- or let me ask you first. Did you make these markings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: What's written in pencil was written by me. I actually circled the number and I wrote what is written in ink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have to object to the foundation. The witness was asked if he's seen this document before, but this document was not a product of his. He simply put markings on it. Could for the record we please know what is the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, ask some questions to lay some foundations for that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who compiled the information on that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Perhaps you mean who typed it all? Do I know that? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. Do you know who showed you the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. You showed me the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is Exhibit P311, and you'll find it in the first of the two intercept binders, which you have been given. And it's simply an index, as you see from the title, of radio and telephone communications. We are not saying that this information has been compiled by the witness, as he just said, but he made, as he explained, reference to these entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry but P311 has not been admitted into evidence. The index has not been proven to be authentic. We still don't know whose creation this was. They've referred that it was part of an Exhibit 311 that has not been admitted into evidence. I think an appropriate question is to ask this witness if he knows who was the source of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can briefly respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness doesn't testify at this point about the accuracy or the contents of this document. He's just marking each line of them and will answer if asked what type of information he has entered in relation to each of these entries. It doesn't go to the content at all of this document, but he can testify what the markings are which he added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just for the record, P311 is an English version, and I take it that -- from looking at it, it seems to coincide with P347, which is also the same English version but with some markings which I understand the gentleman entered. I don't have a B/C/S version and only assume that the gentleman is fluent in English and was able to look at both the English and the B/C/S version in order to comment on this. I'm not sufficiently satisfied with the foundation laid, because it seems that now we're trying to get all of these -- a bundle of intercepts in without a proper foundation. So perhaps Mr. Waespi could just explain a little bit how this document was generated and then what exactly they did before they go into the specific markings. That might give us some indication or some comfort that the gentleman is sufficiently qualified to discuss these matters. And I would like to know whether he reads English and whether he's made a comparison between the English version and the B/C/S version, because as I indicated, we don't have an index in B/C/S, unless one was provided to us and simply we have misplaced it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi. I think you know that P311 is just an index to the intercepted radio and telephone communications. What we want to know is that who prepared this index, whether there is any B/C/S versions of that index.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, as you see, the index is a compilation, basically an assistance to Your Honours, in going through each single intercept which is added to the list. And you see that the users correspond to the people who are mentioned as the participants of each intercept and the summary is briefly the main key parts of the actual intercept. So if you flip through your binder and go to the first exhibit on the tab 25th of June, 1995, you'll see Exhibit 170, and you'll see the users and a brief summary of what the intercept is all about. And I can ask the witness whether he has seen each of these single intercepts, to which he later added remarks on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. My question is that who prepared that index?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And are there any B/C/S versions for that index? These are two very simple questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Mr. President. It's an internal product by the OTP. And second, there is no B/C/S version, but we'll be happy to provide a B/C/S version, because, as you know, the intercepts are in B/C/S. So it would be very easy to transfer the dates and the names of the users and the summary into B/C/S, and that can be done certainly shortly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're just about out of time, and perhaps if we could get together -- if we could take our break now and then we could confer with the Prosecutor, we might be able to find some accommodating position with respect to this. But I'm afraid, short of that, given the answers that I've just heard, I'm not sufficiently satisfied that a foundation can be laid. Because again, unless the gentleman looked at each and every one of these, both in the B/C/S version and in the English version, then the marks that he's making on this particular document, in essence, you know, are suspect. And I'm not suggesting that they're inaccurate in any way, but -- so what I would propose, Your Honour, that we take our break at this point. I think it's just about time, and I would be more than happy to meet with the Prosecutor to see if we can find a way to help in this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, that may be a good idea. So we'll break until 5 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that during the break the problem is solved. Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We had indeed a discussion and got 50 per cent approval. So with your permission, I will ask the witness a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, you have indicated that you met with me and the investigators in my office.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that you were shown this exhibit, which is lying on your desk.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, have you seen each single intercept to which your markings relate to in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And our discussion, was it translated from B/C/S into English and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, it was translated. My handwriting is actually the result of my familiarity with these reproduced messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was it explained to you what the tabs, the headings mean, the tab, date, time, source, users, and indeed the summary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in relation to all these intercepts which you were shown and which you have marked on this exhibit, can you confirm that these were all exhibits that were processed by your unit in summer and autumn 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: All the ones in question were done by my unit, processed by my unit, except one, if I remember rightly. But that one conversation which I marked here with this name of the crypto file is one that was passed on along my communications system to my centre. So that is why I was able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we'll come to that later, but can you tell the Judges briefly what the markings are which you added on the piece of paper, and if you could just explain it on the first marking which relates to tab 173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I hate to object again. We did not come to an agreement over the use of this document. The witness has a notebook which has his original handwriting and his original markings that represent what he remembers and knew and reflected about each one of these intercepts in question. This is just layering on layering without a foundation of information. This is work product from the OTP. The witness's markings may represent 11 out of hundreds of intercepts that represent extraneous information, that, in our opinion, the Prosecutor is trying to back door the information with the summaries to the Trial Chamber at this point. I know that the intercepts have not been ruled on admissible or not admissible, but let's say we skip this one. It's still -- could be admitted into evidence. It's an improper use of work product of the OTP. And yesterday when we tried to introduce the work product of the OTP into evidence, D38, which was an information report, it was not admitted. I think it's an improper foundation. The man has marked markings on something that has been produced by whom he has not testified to. He hasn't said who it's been produced by. He doesn't know. And he has his original document here from which he can testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, I believe that this document is just to facilitate the proceedings and prepared by the Prosecution. It is different from D38. As we ruled yesterday that D38 is kind of proving information which has no evidential value to this court, because we had already heard that witness yesterday. But this one is just an index of all the information. Of course Defence counsel has the right to refer to the original copies of those intercepts in their cross-examination, but to facilitate our work, let us use this index as the basis. And during the proceedings, you may raise any objections you feel -- you deem suitable.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we might not have any objection to the assistance of the OTP with an index list. It's their hearsay summaries that offend the process at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think you know only when we go through all those intercepts at a later stage could we know whether this index is correctly reflected in the contents. It's too early for us to make any rulings on this aspect. So with your cooperation, Ms. Sinatra, we'll let the Prosecution move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I will cooperate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Much obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In relation to the first marking on the first page of this document, that's the fourth entry from above, intercept 173, does that relate to an intercept which you have also seen in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I saw this intercept. This was on the 28th of October, 2003. Based on the elements that have been provided here, the date of the intercept is the one that is stated here, so are the participants stated. And based on my familiarity with the original document which contained the number under which it is registered in the diary that I have, I managed to also convince the Prosecutor that we did generate this document, that it was encrypted in my computer or the computer of my service, that the computer itself during the encryption process determined the eight-digit number that you see. That number has its meaning. And this number below it is the time at which the document was passed on to my centre. So if you permit me now to explain this eight-digit number, you will see that it is a conversation which was conducted on the 10th of July. The first three numbers indicate that it was on the 10th of July. Five indicates the year, 1995. 00 and 16 means the time when the document was encrypted. So it was encrypted on the 10th of July, 1995, at 0016 hours. Underneath I see a number indicating that it was passed on to the centre at 0030 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If we could, please, show to you Prosecution Exhibit 173, and in fact it's /B, the B/C/S version, which would be shown to the witness and /A would be the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this comes out of the first binder of the two intercept binders under tab 9th July, if you flip through P173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is a two-page document. Perhaps if it could be placed on to the ELMO. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document which was generated in my section.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us why you can tell that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I can tell based on the characteristic heading, indicating that it is my service; it has a date, it has a number which is also in the notebook where all the intercepts are recorded; and there are the elements that I mentioned before, if you recall, which are actually those parts which we noted down before the start of every conversation. So at the top we have on the above-mentioned date, we have the frequency, the channel, the time, and we also have the participants in the conversation. So these are all the elements that I talked about earlier. Based on these elements, we formed the sentence which is more or less characteristic for each of our reports. At the end of the conversation, there are the signatures of the people who carried out this task. The first person is the person who recorded the conversation, and the second person is the person who reproduced this conversation or transcribed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, if we could go back to Exhibit P347, which I believe is still on your desk. Now, can you explain us - I think you did already, but just to confirm it - the way you can determine that this specific intercept has been sent to your centre in Tuzla. And if the witness could be given his notebook and also Exhibit 348, which is a five-page copy out of this notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you please repeat the question again for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Witness. If you could determine the time, the actual time this intercept has been sent to your centre in Tuzla. I believe you said it already, you explained it using the exhibit, but I would just like you to tell the Court how you were able to do that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Could you please just give the document back to me that I had earlier so that I could determine this based on the number. I need the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. If P173/B could be given back to the witness. And if it could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. I could most easily determine it based on the number, because in the diary which is an official document, in fact, from that time, they are arranged according to the numbers, the reports in question. So I will find report 526 in the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this would be number 526 which appears on the third line of Prosecution Exhibit P173.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I have this document written down here under number 526. It has been turned into an encrypted file on the 10th of July 1995 at 0016 hours and passed on at 0030 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could now refer to the five copies which have been placed on your desk. If you could find the same page. And perhaps with a marker --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I have just found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- indicate for the record which the numbers are. And if this could be placed on to the ELMO, please. So these green markings correspond to what you have put down in Exhibit 347 for every single intercept. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do have to object to this line of questioning, because from the testimony of the witness before, he stated he received documents from the army unit next to him. He would cut and paste the top of the heading off of the BiH army document and replace it with their document. Then they sent it to their encryption room and it was sent on to Tuzla, to their headquarters. What this represents is this witness does not have personal knowledge of the intercept or the recordings of the intercept, because there's no way that we know which ones he just cut and paste from the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this is a question for you to ask during your cross-examination. If you are not clear with certain points, you have the full right to ask this witness at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the exhibit could be returned and Prosecution Exhibit 192 could be given to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is again from the first binder, tab 12th July, Exhibit 192/B for the witness and /A the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my question for the witness would be: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it even though it's a bad copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could it be placed on the ELMO. Now, why do you recognise the exhibit? What are the elements, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: In this specific case, I can't see the heading. I can't see what the number up is up there. The format of the document is the format that we used, and if you look at the signature, there are persons whom I recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we briefly could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I'm particularly interested in the first conversation, and I'm just reading two or three lines of it. X: Go ahead, General. M: Have these buses and trucks left? X: They have. M: When? X: Ten minutes ago. M: Good, excellent, continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They have all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all, those who want to and those who don't want to. X: I understand, General. Witness, focusing on this particular conversation, there are a number of initials that go down on the left-hand side indicating the participants in the conversation. Now, you talked about that in general terms before the break. Specifically, what does "M" stand for and "X"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I can see that this is a conversation between General Mladic and an unidentified male person. You see in the brackets following General Mladic's name the letter M. So this is why the letter M stands for General Mladic, in order to make the typing itself easier. The male person is X. So every time the male person spoke, we put an X there. We didn't know who the person was and that's why we called the person, person X, unidentified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, General Mladic, he didn't introduce himself or was referred to by the other participant. How were you able to determine that this was General Mladic speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: He was a person who was very much in the public eye. And secondly, we monitored very closely the channel on which he usually spoke. We all were very familiar with his voice, and I don't think we could have mistaken his voice for someone else's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we can return this exhibit, please. If the witness could be shown Prosecution Exhibit 232/D, please. C would be the English, Your Honours, and this is again in the first binder, 14th July. And the witness should also be provided with the three previous pages to this page. In fact, the first page would then be Exhibit 231/D. So four pages. The first page Prosecution Exhibit 231/D and the last one, 232/D. Just to make sure that the witness has received all four pages. Is that correct? Now, Witness, could you again look at the document and tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: This is a document generated by the PEB of the 2nd Corps, a document generated by the military. In these cases, when we obtained a reproduced conversation from them on a floppy, we would just delete their large heading. Their heading would usually take up a lot of space. If you look at some of the originals, it usually took up as much as one-third of the page. In this place we would insert our own number and the date we obtained the conversation. And as you can see, we added a note saying that this conversation was taken over from the BAB of the 2nd Corps, in order to keep the two separate, the documents generated by us and those generated by the military. In addition to that, at the very beginning of the reproduction, their documents never contained the sentence that you almost always find in your documents, using the same elements, the ones you can see here. They have the channel, frequency, and time of conversation, as well as the participant without the usual sentence that we added to the heading. So based on all these elements, I can conclude that this is a document that was obtained from the PEB of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you determine the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: By looking in the notebook and locating the number, I could identify the date when this document was encrypted and sent on. If I look under 626 -- can I just have a moment, please. 626, yes, I can see it. I see that this document was encrypted and crypted on the 15th of July, 1995, at 0037 hours and passed on to my centre at 0040 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If you could now flip to Prosecution Exhibit, and you have it there, 232/D. Now, can you also determine encryption and sending off to the centre of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Based on the elements that I have before me now, I could not determine that. There is no number. This is obviously only a section of an entire file. This is part of the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, looking at all these four pages together, do they contain the same file or are they different parts of the file?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: This is one file. This is one file. It bears a number. And we received it on a floppy in this form. This is an original. The only thing missing is the heading used by the PEB of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So this last conversation we just talked about would have been encrypted when, according to your judgment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: If I look now I see that the last conversation is actually the last conversation of the document marked 626. It was generated, as I read a moment ago, that's when it was generated. It was encrypted. So it's just one file we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. If the exhibit could be returned and we move to the next and, in fact, last exhibit and that would be Prosecution Exhibit 249/B.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Your Honours, that's the second binder for the first time, tab 16th July, Exhibit number 249. And in fact, we do have now, thanks to the Defence, an English translation, and that would be D73/1, although we don't need it for this witness right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that was generated by my section.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us whether it was also forwarded to your superior unit, and if so, when. And just to clarify, I'm particularly interested in the last conversation on that page, that's your number 655.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I can have a look in the notebook. 655 -- I mean, I have this conversation here. It was encrypted in my unit, in my section, on the 16th of July, 1995, at 2004 hours and it was forwarded at 2007 hours. I see that it was encrypted on the 16th of July, 1995, at 1204 hours and registered at 1207 hours. This is an obvious mistake in the way the document was typed, because the conversation was conducted at 1005 hours, and it's only logical that it was encrypted at 1204 hours and forwarded at 1207 hours. It's not the computer making the mistake. Probably it's a mistake generated by the man who typed the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us something about the date which you see on this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: What I see is the 17th of July, 1995. As I said, if I compare this to the time at which the file was encrypted, it is obvious that the person who typed it up made a mistake. This is just one file we're looking at, so we see that of the following documents refer to this date, so there's the same mistake being repeated on a number of occasions within the same file.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if you could turn to the next page and next exhibit, indeed. This is P249/D. It's just the following exhibit in the same intercept file. And again, thanks to the Defence. Defence Exhibit D74/1 will be an English translation of this file. Now, can you look at this document and tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite obvious now. We passed our document on to the military and then just above our heading, they added their own large heading. You can see for yourselves, I was talking about a large heading a moment ago, which we tried to avoid. We would delete it because we had to type these documents out and the heading would normally take up to a third of the page, and this heading meant nothing to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you make a comment on the date of this specific page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I've noticed, this is the same. The date -- you can see for yourselves. The military heading contains the correct date, the 16th of July, 1995, when this was done and forwarded to them. We made a mistake further down, but they simply passed over our mistake and inserted the corrected date, which as we saw in the encrypted file is the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Now, to conclude, if we could go back to Exhibit P347, please. Now, you indicated earlier that there was one document -- one intercepted conversation which you couldn't determine. And I would like you to refer to page 16 of this document. And it's the line -- the third from above the number 298. Page 16, 298. And I would like you to have a look at the exhibit 298, please. And while we are doing that, I see that there is no numbers on the date in this exhibit. Can you tell us why you weren't able to determine when it was encrypted, this specific intercept. And if the usher could please show to the witness Prosecution Exhibit 298/B.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this, Your Honours, would be again the second binder, 25th of July. And it would be helpful if a version could be put on to the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: My first question: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us if this document was sent to your centre in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Based on the elements that I have in front of me, I cannot determine that. The only comment I can offer is that this is obviously a part of a military file. I can see that there is a prior conversation that was done by the army. So probably when we gave them the floppy they just pasted our conversation into their file and sent it off. In order for me to be able to determine when it was encrypted, I should have its file number. This should be the original copy of the document that we sent from our own communications centre. Based on that number, I could determine that. As things are, I can't determine anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you can say that this was a document which was processed by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. The other conversation beginning on a certain frequency and a given channel at a certain time, that is one of our documents. That's our document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last point on page 14 of Prosecution Exhibit 317 -- 347 page 14. The second to last entry from the bottom is 284. And I see a question mark there at the second number. Page 14 of this document number 284, question mark. Can you explain that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I could try to explain if you give me the document back to see the file number. This will help me to trace it in the notebook and see why I added 1930 hours there -- well, I don't think I was certain about the specific time when this document was forwarded to my centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit 284, then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: 19, 18 of July, 19 -- 09, 62 -- yes, yes, I have it. That's it. There were several files that were being forwarded at the same time. In my logbook, in this notebook, it's quite illegible, but what it probably means is 1930 hours, so I can't be certain, however, since it's unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to summarise, for all these exhibits which you were able to see in my office, bar the two examples we mentioned, you were able to determine the exact date and time it was encrypted in your computer and sent to your centre in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. I am not able to determine anything without looking at the actual document. Based on the number, I can trace it back to my notebook and tell you the exact time when it was encrypted and sent on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's what you have done while we were sitting together in my office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Any cross-examination, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. And if you want to move to the front, please do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand it, you've been in the security service since -- the state security service since 1982. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I also understand that during the period that we're discussing that you were working on intercepting messages.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And though you were in essence working independently, there were occasions when you would share material.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Not just occasionally. We exchanged all the conversations or shared all the conversations from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I understand that your procedure was slightly different from theirs in that you did not have notebooks as they did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: The procedure was the same. When I say "the same," what I mean is that this is a procedure that you must follow if you're in that line of work. It's just that we didn't have our own notebooks where we copied the conversations. We had loose papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, sir. However, nothing prevented you from collecting those loose sheets of paper so that today, perhaps, we could look at the handwritten notes and compare them with the type-written notes that were then encrypted and sent off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: You're quite right, however, back in 1994 we didn't know that one day there would be a Tribunal. Secondly, and this is what decided us, we worked in a location that was a remote location far from any settled areas. It wasn't sufficiently secure. What we were taught in your line of work was: If something wasn't sufficiently secured, you had to burn it after you'd passed it on because otherwise all the information would have been given away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, because -- I take it during that period there was also a shortage of tapes, and so the tapes had to be recycled, in other words, used over and over again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: There were cases like that. Sometimes we believed that certain conversations were not particularly relevant and there was no need to preserve those. So we would just rewind the tape and tape over those conversations. However, whenever we had something that we thought was particularly relevant, we would copy all these conversations on a single tape. And once the tape was full, it was forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I guess, could I just describe those as sort of the best of the intercepts? Let me clarify it. The ones that you would copy would be the ones that you had screened and deemed to be sort of the best of the messages that you had listened to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. We would assess what was interesting, because we are qualified to make that assessment and to tell our superiors, that is, we had the full freedom to make such an assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, can I conclude that part of your job was also to make an analysis of the messages, or were you merely capable because of your experience to screen out what was basically relevant and what was not relevant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: We didn't make any analysis of the classic type, but in our diaries, we would write down the frequency and the channel which would be particularly interesting. We would describe to the people who would follow us that such and such a person appeared there, that they should pay attention to him, that in the previous period there were such and such conversations, and that they should strictly take care of that channel. Especially when the other two people came, then several hours would be spent on explaining what had happened over the past few days so that we could direct them in some way. But then some of the conversations would also be recorded in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when -- listening in on a conversation, did you ever use the pause button where, for instance, part of the conversation was not terribly interesting or relevant? Did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: If I were to use the pause, then I would stop at a moment when I had heard enough to write that down. If it wasn't interesting enough, I would press pause, but I would let it pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it that the machine that you were using, when you used pause, it actually stopped the tape as opposed to allow you to continue listening to the conversation, and then the pause not recording what was actually being said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: You are asking me something else now. I understood that you were asking me during the reproduction process of the conversation, not during the taping process. This is what I understood you to be asking me. When I'm reproducing the conversation, when I'm writing it down, then I would press pause to write down what I remembered. Then I would depress pause again and continue, then I would press again right down. When recording there's no reason for me to press the pause button, although if I deemed the conversation that I had just recorded not to be interesting, then I could play back the tape or I would continue to record another conversation, and then later when there was time, I could rewind the tape back to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me rephrase my question and thank you for clarifying the point. But it's my understanding with the recording devices as the one that you and your colleagues from the army were using, even though you would press the pause button, it would merely stop the recording process but would still allow the listener to hear the conversation, thus allowing the listener to discriminate what he wanted to record or not record.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Excellent. Yes, that's how it was. Because if we were to stop recording on the UHER, we were listening to it at the same time over the radio device that had already decoded the signal, and then it would be recorded but we would hear it. So if a man was talking to his girlfriend, we would not record that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Precisely, that's the point I wanted to make. And thank you. Now, my next question, it has to do with a particular word that you used and I want to make sure that I totally understand what you meant. You indicated on direct examination that you wanted to make sure that what you were transcribing was authentic. That was the word that you used.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: We strived for the ideal, not because of the participants, I said they were not important to us. Very often we didn't know those people, but because of the events. The events that were ongoing were very important to us. So we would try with all our might for the document to be authentic so that the people who were analysing this document when it got to them, there is no dilemma. We were not allowed to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I guess in English that word may have a different connotation. So my question is: Are you suggesting what you were trying to do is be accurate on what you heard in transcribing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: We were accurate. If we heard it, we wrote it down. If we did not hear it, we would put down three points. If we heard it, we would put an X. If we didn't hear it, we would put a Y. If we heard something but we were not sure of what we heard, then we would put a question mark in parenthesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I ask the question because if, for instance, we're speaking about a particular person's voice, there might be an occasion where you would say this is the authentic voice of that individual versus this is an accurate version of what we heard. Do you see the distinction that I'm trying to make?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I will try to explain.
