If I am on such and such a frequency and on such and such a channel I know that only you would pick up or somebody close to you, and then you would pick up the phone. I know your voice. I already know that you're there. So if you respond, I know that it is you. I know that no one else would respond to your mobile telephone. But if the courier picked up the telephone, and I don't know who he is, and in the conversation he would say he is a courier, then I would put down that he is was a courier. I wouldn't know his name, but I know that he picked up the phone from the office of Mladic. I know that, so I can tell my superiors that that is what it was definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. One last question regarding this area. And I'm going to use a term which I believe perhaps is more accurate than the one that some of us use here in court, the raw tape, the tape itself that was the original, the one that was actually being used by you, so if we could use the term "raw tape." As far as I understand, you do not have any of those raw tapes in your possession at this moment as we speak regarding the intercepts that we're discussing here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I first have to inform you that I'm no longer doing these tasks and I no longer have them in my possession. But had I at that time passed on any raw tape, as you term it, yes, I did. But then it became a problem because of the quantity of the tapes, and then we made an effort to transfer all of those raw tapes to one tape, because we had a problem with paper. But of course we also had a problem with tapes, a shortage of tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I could switch over to another topic with respect to the particular notebook that you've been discussing here earlier. Was it only you filling in this notebook or were your colleagues filling it in as well when, for instance, you might have been resting or off shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, it was an official document which contained the elements which were there, and these elements were entered by each operator who would pass on the data, who participated in the processing of each document. When he completed the job, he would receive confirmation that the document was received at the destination, and then amongst the elements that were noted down in the notebook would say report, such and such, encrypted as such and such, was passed on at such and such a time. I did fill in several such reports, but I did the least number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were asked to look at one particular exhibit which is number 249, and that is the one that we seem to have some discrepancy with respect to the date. Do you recall that one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. I think that I do remember it, and I think that it has a military heading, and it's dated 16th of July, if I can remember it well. And then underneath it is our date, the 17th of July. I don't know if you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can see it. Thank you. In your particular version of it, the one that was generated by your outfit, typed out, it seems to also indicate on the first one, which would be 652, it would -- it starts with: "On the day in question." If we could provide you with a copy of it, perhaps it would help you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the gentleman could be shown 249/B. And I'm referring to in the English version, I'll refer to the Defence Exhibit which is D73/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could look at that, it seems that there are several intercepts and you've numbered them from 652 to 655. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I see it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at the ones starting with 652, it begins with the -- by stating: "On the day in question," and it goes on to give us the frequency and the channel and the hour. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we were to go all the way to 655, we see the phrase: "The same day on the same frequency," and it says the channel and so on. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you don't -- I take it you were not the one that had actually taken down this message?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I did not generate this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe I heard you earlier indicating that you did not type out the text either. You didn't -- well, you didn't receive it. What I meant in my first question, and forgive me for being inarticulate, you did not receive it, write it out. And my next question is: You didn't type it out either. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I didn't understand you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me break it down. Sitting here today, do you know whether you were the individual listening in on this conversation and then taking it down and writing it out before it was actually typed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I did not do this, this that I'm looking at now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me make sure that I understand it correctly. Does the same person who listens in on the conversation and then writes it down on the pieces of paper that you've indicated, is that normally the same person that would then have it typed and encrypted before it goes off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: It's not usually, but that is not a rule. Below at the end of the text you have two people who are signed. The first person, I explained that before, is the person who recorded the document. The second person is the person who reproduced the document. Who sent it out, you can usually tell by the signature. We didn't record that separately, but you could tell by the handwriting, because there were only four people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But in looking at this particular document now today that you have in front of you, can you tell us -- can you identify -- you don't need to mention the person's name, but can you identify the individual that actually listened in to the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The person who listened and recorded this conversation is the first person. The second person reproduced this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you can identify from looking at this piece of paper who those individuals are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: When I see a signature, I can tell who it is, because they signed in code. Their signatures are encrypted, but by their handwriting, I know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But do you see their signatures on this document? I guess that's what I'm asking you. There is some writing on the document. And what I'm asking you, and you don't have to identify the individuals, but looking at the document, this what we have, can you tell us whether you know who those two individuals are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Very well, of course. I do, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, other than this notebook that you have, is there any other material that you can share with us that would give us -- that would tell us exactly when this message was received and when it was encrypted and sent out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: There is only one other way in which I could convince you, and that is if I checked back at my firm, whether they still have the coded files in code form under this number. I know when all of these files are decoded, they keep the same file name. So when you look at the decoded file, which I know exists in the service, then you would determine that that is indeed it. So this is the only other way to do it. But at the moment it's not possible for me to use this other method.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one last question. When you said the firm, your firm, I assume you're working today for the same organisation that you were working back then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it your firm, or the firm as we would call it elsewhere, has made that material available to the Prosecution for their inspection, and if necessary, for their collection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: This is done by the authorised persons. I'm a technical person who was up there doing their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have questions. Would you like to take the break now or would you like for me to go forward? I just need to grab the podium because I can't see that far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How long will your cross-examine last, more or less?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: More or less 30 to 40 minutes. It depends on the answers from the witness, Your Honour, also. You know, I don't know how long he's going to give -- how long his answers are going to be, so I predict 30 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you have to remember sometimes you cannot get whatever answers you want from a witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I am very familiar with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's take the break and resume at 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Sir, you've received orders from your command to focus on certain issues and certain features that you were monitoring. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: In addition to receiving an order to gather intelligence, I didn't get anything more specific than that --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you on the right channel?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Number 4. Maybe it's a technical problem. I'm not sure. I saw Mr. Waespi turning his mike off when he was questioning and because there's extra protections with the witness, maybe there's some clue that I'm not sure of -- if I leave this open ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that if you do that, the voices get mixed. So you need to turn it off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We try it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'll try it again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you received orders from your command headquarters explaining to you what your focus of your monitoring should be. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I did not receive any orders in a written form --

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Even with the microphone off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, there may be some technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I could move up there. Maybe I should see if I can hear anything from the interpretation booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I can hear you now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Sir, I don't remember if you remember my question, but instead of asking again, could I just hear your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. I've already tried several times to begin my answer. I did not receive specific orders. Before I went to that location, my duty was to gather intelligence, all the intelligence that I could obtain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. But you were aware that on July 14th and 15th, 1995, you had been ordered to focus on the fleeing Bosnian Muslims of 10.000 soldiers, women and children, who were trying to escape to Tuzla from Srebrenica. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I really did not have an order. Let me put it this way: It's typical of the military chain of command, but it didn't pertain to my service. We were taught to identify intelligence ourselves and to prioritise, to assess what was more or less relevant. It was up to us to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. So you're saying that these 10.000 people running for their lives was not a concern of the association or the firm that you're with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: No. That's not what I'm saying, not at all. I did gather intelligence and I forwarded the intelligence obtained. But I don't think I fully understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: The natural focus of your monitoring situation would have been a concern for the security services, the state security services, for the well-being of 10.000 of its citizens, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Among other things, we monitored and tried to obtain intelligence that throughout this entire period was related to people who were moving through the woods and so on and so forth. Everything that was related to intelligence or any intelligence that may have been essential for my work, I would record it and forward it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. You were an amateur radio operator that became chief of an anti-electronic war unit. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: No. I was an employee of the service, and then I became head of that unit. But I've been a radio amateur since I turned 14. You're quite right in claiming that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want to ask you based on your expertise in anti-electronic warfare, at the time you were aware of Operativno Maskiranje, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. It's part of the theory of electronic surveillance and anti-electronic warfare. I am familiar with the term of masking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Right. And masking includes misinformation, decoying, planting fake conversations, and supplying false data and false names, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Obviously. You seem well informed. That's in theory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And also, there are other methods of obstructing interceptions, right, such as encryption, switching channels, channel switching as they call it, changing your codes and your code names that you use in times of combat. Those are common methods of obstructing interception, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the equipment that you identified earlier, it was a picture of a Kenwood, but what was that Kenwood? Was it a transceiver or a receiver? Can you explain what that Kenwood was, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: The device depicted in that photograph is a Kenwood TR-7000. It's a receiver. It's not a transceiver.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So basically you had one set of equipment in your room with a two-man shift. It was a scanner with a hand-made, home-made device hooked to the antenna with another connecter to an UHER recorder. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Can you please clarify. What was home-made?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I believe you stated that the connector from your Kenwood scanner was a home-made box that was connected to the antenna. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Precisely. It was hand-made but not home-made. It was not professionally manufactured. It was not bought from a factory or a specialised shop. This was put together by people in a workshop who were qualified to put together this piece of equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. You also I don't think ever explained to us exactly, you have four men at your position at one time. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And two men serving shifts of 24 hours each?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Not 24 hours. Two men would spend several days at a time. And then another two men would come to relieve them, and then they would also spend several days there, depending on the work load. We made assessments whether it would be two days, five days, or a maximum of seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Okay. So I believe what you're telling me is you didn't have four men present at the unit at all times, you had two men present for anywhere from a four- to seven-day shift. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: It is correct that I always had two men there while the other two were resting, but this depended on the work load and how tired the men were. Their shift would sometimes last two days, but sometimes the shift lasted seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you were part of that two-man shift. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I was not part of the permanent crew. I was the head of that particular unit. I had other tasks and duties. Until mid-June, I had been spending less time there, but when the gathering of intelligence intensified, when the whole thing was stepped up, I was around to help.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And that reminds me, when you say when the activities were stepped up or the monitoring was stepped up, there was extremely heavy radio traffic from the end of June until the end of July, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I can explain this. When we talk about those radio frequencies, there were always conversations going on, but depending on what was happening on the ground, sometimes the intensity of the intelligence coming in was higher or lower, depending on what specifically was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, I just asked you the end of June through the end of July, the radio traffic was extremely heavy during that time, wasn't it, because there was a lot going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot more intelligence at that time, a lot more intelligence relevant to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, I just want to get this clear, too. When you say "intelligence," intelligence doesn't mean that you got some secret information. It means that you were just receiving more traffic on the radio waves when you were at Okresanica. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: A lot more information. A lot more intelligence indicating certain developments that were of interest to us at the time. I will try to clarify this. If you look at the military aspect, once combat operations are under way, then there's a lot of intelligence going on. And every single piece of information that you can lay your hands on is essential, which makes you more dedicated to your work throughout such periods.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Didn't give you more men to back up your position with, did it, or give you more equipment to monitor 24 frequencies, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Well, at that time my service could only spare so many men or so much equipment. It was certainly a pity that more men could not be spared at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I want to ask you now about the UHER recorder that you were describing and you identified a picture of. What we know is in the one room that you shared with two men for a four- to seven-day shift or that comprised, made up of two men, the UHER recorder that you identified, you had one set of equipment during this time, right, one receiver, scanner, and one recorder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: That's not correct. Would you like me to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: How many receivers did you have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I had three combinations, what we called combinations. Now, what's a combination? I tried to explain before. A combination would assist of an antenna, a converter, a radio receiver, and a reel-to-reel recorder. The next combination would normally be another receiver and another reel-to-reel recorder. The third combination would normally be yet another receiver, yet another reel-to-reel. And we had another reel-to-reel recorder which we used to play back the tapes which was separate from these sets. It wasn't connected to the other sets.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Let me just ask you. When you had two men up there for a seven-day shift, there was one person working 24 hours at a time, and then the other person would take over. It would be impossible for that one person to use more than one set of equipment. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I would be a very poor chief of section to work in this way. That's not how it worked. There were two men working from morning to evening and at night. During the night, there was usually a lull and everyone would try to get some sleep. You saw the reports and the last of the reports would usually be sent just after midnight, sometimes a little later, but normally the men would then try to get some sleep late in the evening, both of them. One of the men was operating one of the combinations, and one of the sets, combinations, was always kept on the frequency of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. And the other man meanwhile was operating the other combination being used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So you had what we call banking hours. Two men worked side by side on a shift and then they both took a rest and went to bed. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I want to ask you about -- the attorney for Blagojevic had asked you about raw material, raw tape. There are no raw tapes that you know of that existed in your unit from July 1995 that exist today. Is that correct? That you know of.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't say anything about that. You should talk to some other people, those who actually have these tapes in their safe. Let me repeat this: I was the person who carried out this work, and I just passed it on. But then there were other people who processed everything after I had passed it on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: But during this process of preparing to testify, you haven't heard any raw tape from your unit or any unit at Okresanica from -- July 1st through July 30th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: One thing I know is that there were tapes. I don't know what the Tribunal actually has. I don't have this information. It's not my job. If there was a specific conversation that was played back to me, perhaps I could tell you something about it. But only if you played to me, then I can tell you something.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Sir, I just asked if you had heard one during your preparation. It is a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to the equipment that you were using. Did you maintain that equipment yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: With the exception of some very few cases when the belt on the UHER broke, we had no other cases where repairs were needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And by belt you mean the Mylar magnetic tape that y'all used. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: No, the belt. Inside the UHER there is a belt that conveys the revolutions from the engine, the motor itself to the reel. When we used it several times it happened that the belt broke and we fixed it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I understand. It's like a belt on a vacuum cleaner. But when it was down, do you remember what month it was that your recorder was broken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I don't. I can't specify the time for any of these occurrences. I'm talking about the belt breaking. It would only take a few minutes for us to fix it and then we would just go ahead as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So you didn't maintain any maintenance logs on your equipment either, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: No. This was not our obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, you discussed earlier in your testimony your procedure for recording. I just want a yes or no answer. The truth is there are no recordings from your activities at Okresanica in 1995. Right? That you know of. You haven't heard any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I know there are some. I'm certain about this. Now, how many are there, what does the Tribunal have in its possession, I can't say. But I know that we made those and we sent them on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you destroyed all of your handwritten notes or rough notes that you took down in writing. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And you didn't keep any notebooks where the content of any conversations were transcribed into, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: As I said before, we did our best to pass on to the centre everything that we typed into our computer. Then we would receive confirmation that they had received what we had sent on to them. Then after a day, after one day, we would just destroy the whole lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So the answer is yes to my question, there are no handwritten notes reflecting the content of any conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: We have not preserved the transcripts of those conversations because we burnt them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. And so what we have here is a notebook that you brought to the Tribunal, which is a log of a record of your -- when a message was sent to your encryption department and when it was sent on to your command. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. This was our duty, our responsibility, to keep those records and when the information was encrypted and sent on, with the contents as you can see them in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And I believe you testified earlier that what you did was you took the intercept information from the army. You, what we call, cut and paste. You cut off its heading, you pasted it on your heading, and you forwarded it on to your encryption department and then on to your headquarters. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. But in addition to that, we added a single sentence at the top of the page indicating that the document or the report was obtained from the PEB of the 2nd Corps. We didn't pass this on, because we had all of that in front of us on our desk. When you say sending it on to the communications centre and encrypting it there, we encrypted this information right where we were, because we had it all there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: What I'm trying to explain is that you received the message from the army, you encrypted it yourself, and then you sent it on to your headquarters. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And for those intercepts, you have no personal knowledge of the contents of those intercepts. You put a header on it, you gave it a summary, but it was a summary of a summary of the army recordings. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Well, yes. Very often we did not read those reports, we just sent it on. We had no time for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you. So the notebook that you brought here is really just a representation of when you encrypted a message and when it was sent. It has nothing to do with the contents of the message itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Nothing whatsoever indicates the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And that also goes for P232, which was an exhibit that you reviewed earlier, which represents your notes that were the notes of the -- as indicated of Bosnian army that you sent on to your headquarters. Right? P232 was recorded on July 14th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I was just trying to save time as the Prosecutor has done by his indexes. But I would like to ask you. You have been very forthcoming in your information here. The truth is that you would never be able to have a voice identification or know the voice of Dragan Jokic, would you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: That's correct. I could not identify his voice unless he introduced himself, of course, or unless one of military came along and told us that's that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Any re-direct, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are there any documents to tender at this stage? Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, there are, Mr. President. The Exhibit P319, that's the colour photo of a radio. Then P320, that's a photo of the UHER. Then I guess in relation to P347, the index to the intercepts we'll have that share the fate of all the other intercepts. I think it's really specific to this witness, but we can be patient and wait for that. In relation to P347, the five pages of the notebook, Defence has suggested they would like to copy the whole notebook. I personally don't have a problem, but it's not my notebook, obviously, but the witness's. And since he -- and much of it is empty. So I'm not entirely sure whether that assists the Trial Chamber with any other pages of it, whose contents I really don't know other than the five pages which contain these numbers. So I leave it to Your Honours how to deal with it. If it becomes too complicated, I wouldn't use it as an exhibit at all because he explained the procedure and told how it went. But I would suggest just to admit the five pages -- perhaps even only the one page on which he marked something in relation to Exhibit 173. And lastly, the piece of paper, P353 with his name on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And the last document is -- I think is 350.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That may well be. I may have confused something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, 353. It's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections or comments? Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll start with my comments first, Your Honour. With the exception of the notebook, I have no objections. With respect to the notebook or the pages from the notebook, I do object. First, there are only five pages. Secondly, the notebook hasn't been translated. We would ask, one, that if they so wish to introduce anything from the notebook, that, one, the entire notebook be copied; secondly, that it be translated. But aside from that, I'm not confident that a sufficient foundation was laid, particularly after listening to the cross-examination by Ms. Sinatra and portions of mine, but I would say that the lion's share of my loss of confidence in the foundation is based on the cross-examination done by Ms. Sinatra. It's uncertain whether this gentleman was there during the critical period of time when these notations were made, particularly the ones that the Prosecution is most interested in. We are not certain, and it has not been clarified, that this gentleman was the one that actually made the notations in the book. So he cannot give any verification. All he can say is that he was the commander of this unit, if I can use that term, or komandir, or section chief, whatever we use. But other than that, he has not been involved in that process. He cannot give us any assurances that it was done in the same procedure each and every time. We know that there have been errors. And it would -- I'm particularly concerned given that there were only four individuals, two shifts, and in light of the shifts and the length of time of the shifts, it would seem to me that the notebook itself or the contents in the notebook are suspect. Also, he did indicate that by looking at a particular number he could tell when something was sent off, but yet we have nothing else to verify that. So I am afraid unless I can be persuaded, and there may be a persuasive argument from the Prosecution or from the Trial Bench, I'm afraid that I would have to register an objection to the five pages or even the entire notebook being introduced with the lack of -- or with the foundation as it stands today. So that's my position. I hope I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sinatra, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I join in, of course, the objection by the counsel for Blagojevic. I believe that there was an improper foundation laid. We don't know whether he was even present during the days that we are talking about that he has notated in his book. We don't know whether the book is full of his handwriting or someone else's or whether it was just a log kept in the unit. So I think there is an improper foundation. I just wanted to clarify, is it my understanding that -- that's P348. P347 was withdrawn by the Prosecutor at this time for admission? I don't think he tendered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Not withdrawn, but I thought we agreed upon that all the intercept-related exhibits would be admitted once the legal arguments were finalised. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. As for the other documents, you have no objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I just want to clarify, if I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: When he says he's just not tendering it at the moment, he's tendering it but subject to the ruling by the Court on the intercepts or he's going to wait and tender it after the ruling by the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think Mr. Waespi told us that he will wait until a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since we still have the witness here and since both Defence teams claim that there is something unclear about that document, Mr. Waespi, could you take the opportunity to ask some more questions concerning this document towards this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. If the witness could be shown the notebook. I want to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sir, whose notebook is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Just in the spirit of true professional gamesmanship, I just want to clarify that once we've passed the witness and we have no further questions of him and we argue over whether the proper foundation had been laid by the Prosecutor, then they get another bite at authenticating their documents? I'm just trying to get whether we have the same rights sometime in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course. That's why we have the witness here when we -- concerning whether to admit a document or not. That's just to give the witness the opportunity to explain to us those questions raised by either parties. Of course, you know, you will have the full right to cross-examine this witness on that particular point. And of course in the future you have the same right to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for clarifying that. I appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, just for clarification, I did not ask to re-examine this witness. I believe we have laid enough foundation because of the questions he -- the answers he gave in direct examination, and I believe you have asked me to ask a few questions because the witness is still here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course. Just for the sake of the Trial Chamber as well as for the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sir, the notebook in front of you, to whom does it belong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: It's the diary which was in the electronic surveillance centre of the state security service at the Okresanica location from 1994 until the end of our stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in whose possession has it been since 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: It was at the section in that one room on the desk, and we used it to note down the numbers, as I mentioned before, as is appropriate for a correctly managed logbook. We cannot say that this is really a communications centre, since there were very few people there, we unified this. So this was the logbook which recorded all the information that had been sent out. On the other hand, there was also a notebook where information was noted about the electronic surveillance of certain directions. For example, if we direct our antenna towards the south and monitor the frequencies or scan the frequencies there, all the data that we receive or acquire in that period, we note down here. After a while, if we assess that something is interesting, we stay there; if not, we continue on. Here you have the exact dates. For example, that on the 4th of June, 1995, we have a note by one of the workers who was scanning. Then on the 7th of June, 1995, and then -- just one moment, please. It's a little bit untidy, but it's still quite possible to find one's way. On the 7th of June, also we have more. On the 22nd of August, we also have something. On the 25th of August, we have something. So this is a workbook. On the other side of the logbook, since we had a shortage of paper, indicating in this period when we were sending out this information also noted down the scans. For example, on one route we noted down eight working channels which were active. So it's quite clear what is written down here. For example, channel 1 it says, "Extension 837, Panorama." And we know that Panorama was the location of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. Then channel 02, the telephone and telegraph messages were recorded from Badem one. This is a pseudonym for one of their communication centres, for one of their locations. Then there is a phone number of an exchange on channel 5, 786545. So this is a telephone extension which you can dial from town. Then on channel 7 we recorded that there was a city telephone number 783785. We have some other numbers here which were linked to the persons who were then important in Republika Srpska. So I don't want to go through all of them. We have information about them. When you were talking about whether to copy the entire logbook, I suggest that you can copy that, you can copy sections of the logbook or the notebook. Unfortunately, like all human beings, the people who worked there have some personal notes and remarks in the workbook. For example, they have some -- for example, they say "pearls," they heard a funny sentence as they were listening, so they noted that down. So this is nothing more than than some sort of personal comment in those difficult times, but you can clearly determine who it was by the handwriting. My handwriting is there, the handwriting of my colleagues also. In this other part in the logbook, also you will see that there is the handwriting there of the people who wrote that down, and my handwriting is also amongst them. The conversations that we presented here, amongst them there are those that I personally recorded. So this is as much as I can say regarding this logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have some questions to you, Mr. Waespi. When did you get this diary, this notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can ask the witness when he provided it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot this logbook. It came subsequently. I cannot remember the exact date, but I think it was a day before I made remarks in the evidence based on the logbook. The next day we analysed the report of the past -- on intercepts, and I could say that they were done on such and such a day. This is something that can be determined only based on the crypto file, encryption file. For a time our computers, when I would send the computer to the communications centre, at the end of the file there would be a date and also the time. I don't know where these files are, but this is enough proof that this was done in such a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you disclose this earlier, to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, we did. The five pages with these numbers on it, we did disclose it to the Defence the same day, I believe, or a day later. I have seen the notebook for the first time. And to clarify when the witness came in on the weekend, that was the weekend prior to last weekend, he indicated that he had a notebook at home which may solve a couple of our questions. So he asked that his office in Tuzla, a colleague of his would write to Sarajevo, and then it was processed from Sarajevo to The Hague. And that's the first time we saw this -- I personally saw this notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I may have a moment. For the record, Your Honour, I am told that we got the several pages with the proofing notes from the Prosecution. That's when we received the five pages, but if I can move, Your Honour, and I'm going to need to look at the notebook very briefly, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps in the meantime I can tell that the correspondence which Mr. Karnavas mentioned when we gave these five pages to the Defence was on the 31st of October, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could take a look at the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you bring this notebook the first time when you testified in the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, I did bring it. I didn't bring it this time, because my briefcase at that time was lost in the airplane. It had been opened, and I received it after a week. I had received a new briefcase, because my old one was damaged. So this time I didn't bring it because I was afraid that somebody would take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that this was brought over from Tuzla. Was this in your personal possession the entire time or was it stored someplace?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: It was stored in a safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who has the key to the safe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I had the key.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it was stored with you, not by somebody else? You kept it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And is there a particular reason why you are in possession of a certain evidence that belongs to a section that you no longer work for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: If we were to talk now about my business engagement, then I would like to ask the Court to move to a private session. But the logbook, just as in my statement which was given, I don't remember anymore which year, it was used. That's why it remained in the safe. So as a document in the service, it's not such an important document. It is important only to you. We don't need it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if that were the case, is there a particular reason why you didn't leave this document -- this notebook with the Prosecution two or three years ago when you were here testifying for the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: There's no need for that. It was returned to me. I took it back, and then things occurred as I explained. So I just simply took it back and stored it. It wasn't used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and if I understood you correctly, there are actually two notebooks within this -- two different sets of records in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: You can see that for yourself in the logbook. Precisely at the place where you have your hand it says: Record of information sent out, I think. And then on the other side there are notes which were actually the written notes of electronic surveillance, the monitoring of the frequencies. And that contains all the information that is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With respect to the particular intercepts that we discussed here today, did you make notations with respect to those intercepts in this notebook, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Yes. There are some places where I did that personally, and I can indicate those to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me make sure you understood my question correctly. There were several intercepts that were discussed here today that you had the opportunity to initial in the English version of the index. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: Of course, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With respect to those particular intercepts that are numbered, did you make the notations yourself in the book, in this -- did you make the record of those particular intercepts, or were they made by your colleagues, your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: I would have to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. We'll get to that. The next question is: Did you as the chef, the chief of this little operation, did you conduct any quality control measures to make sure that what was put down by your subordinates matched what had happened? And if so, what were those quality control measures that you had in place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That question is out of the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Well, if that is the case, Your Honour, then I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I have two questions, Your Honour, maybe one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: You stated just then under re-cross that this notebook was only important to Mr. Karnavas, as counsel for Blagojevic. Didn't you just state that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your exact words were: It's important only to you. That's the exact testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: When I say "you," it's a pseudonym, meaning this Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: And knowing that this notebook was important to this Honourable Court, you chose to leave it in your safe back in your country. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: In my first statement which I gave, I provided this logbook. So I didn't think that it would be a good idea to destroy it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: So your answer is knowing that this was important to the Tribunal, you chose, you made the decision, to leave it in your safe. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-118
utterances.text: That's right. Knowing that it was important for this Court, I left it in the safe for safe keeping.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Waespi, do you want to ask something?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, first of all I would like to say that document P319, P320, and P353 are admitted into the evidence. As for this document, we believe that we only need what is relevant in that diary. And this Tribunal is only concerned with any information which is related to this case but not other matters. So we would like to ask the registrar to make a copy of that diary and keep it in the possession of the Registrar. Then we will give it, the copy, to the parties, but not all of this notebook is admitted into the evidence. Only those five pages tendered by the Prosecution are admitted into the evidence. It's so decided. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. I'm sorry that we have kept you here for quite a long time, but I'm sure that tomorrow morning we'll send you back home. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And, Witness, before you are leaving, please send this diary to the registrar which is sitting there in front of you. I can assure you that he will return that diary to you before you take your flight tomorrow morning. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 6.44 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of November, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 25
